## Where we are

- **slides-01** *(this deck)* — Enformer architecture deep dive: the 3-part design, receptive fields, and how predictions emerge
- **slides-02** — Borzoi, AlphaGenome, and the next generation of sequence-to-function models

---

## The promise of the Human Genome

In 2000, President Clinton announced the completion of the human genome draft:

> *"This will revolutionize the diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of most, if not all, human diseases."*

::: {.source-credit-linked}
Francis Collins, 2000
:::

The promise was bold — and partially fulfilled. But there was a surprise:

---

## The surprise: knowing the sequence wasn't enough

We sequenced the genome. We found the genes. But:

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**What we learned:**

- ~20,000 protein-coding genes
- The sequence varies between individuals
- GWAS found hundreds of thousands of disease-associated loci
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**What we still didn't know:**

- Which gene a GWAS variant actually affects
- Why most disease variants sit in **non-coding** regions
- How the same DNA sequence produces different cell types
:::
:::

---

## Most disease variants are in non-coding DNA

![](img/2026-05-04-DNA-seq-to-epigenome-applications_0.png)
![](img/2026-05-04-DNA-seq-to-epigenome-applications_1.png)

::: {.source-credit-linked}
[EBI GWAS Training Course](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/online/courses/gwas-catalogue-exploring-snp-trait-associations/)
:::

---

## Why non-coding variants matter

GWAS loci are thought to act by altering **transcription factor binding**:

> Albert, F., Kruglyak, L. The role of regulatory variation in complex traits and disease. Nat Rev Genet 16, 197–212 (2015).

::: {.source-credit-linked}
Albert & Kruglyak, 2015
:::

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**The problem:**

- A SNP in a non-coding region changes a TF binding motif
- This alters gene expression
- This changes disease risk
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**The challenge:**

- We can't easily measure TF binding for every variant in every cell type
- ChIP-Seq costs thousands of dollars per sample
- We need ~100+ samples for population-level studies
:::
:::

---

## The TWAS approach — "PrediXcan 1.0"

Instead of measuring expression directly, **predict** it from genotype:

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Step 1:** Train a model to predict gene expression from DNA sequence using reference panels (GTEx)

**Step 2:** Apply the model to GWAS data to find which genes' predicted expression associates with disease
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Advantages:**

- Reduced multiple testing (10⁶ SNPs → 20K genes)
- Direction of effect (up or down regulation)
- Identifies candidate causal genes
:::
:::

---

## But TWAS has limitations

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**What works well:**

- Highly heritable genes
- Well-annotated tissues with large sample sizes
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**What doesn't:**

- Low heritability genes (often the most disease-relevant)
- Tissues that are hard to sample (brain, pancreas)
- Cross-ancestry prediction (poor transfer)
- Rare variation (missed by linear models)
:::
:::

---

## Can deep learning help?

Traditional TWAS uses **linear models** (elastic net) to predict expression from SNPs.

**What if we replace the predictor with a deep learning model?**

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Deep learning advantages:**

- Learns complex sequence patterns (motifs, combinatorial rules)
- Can predict from raw DNA sequence — no SNP preprocessing needed
- One model → predictions for thousands of outputs
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**The key question:**

> Can we predict **any** epigenomic signal — not just gene expression — from raw DNA sequence?
:::
:::

---

# Part 1: The Enformer Model {background-color="#1e3a5f" style="color:white;"}

---

## Enter Enformer

Enformer (Avsec et al., Nat Methods 2021) predicts **thousands of epigenomic tracks** from DNA sequence alone:

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Predicts:**

- DNase-Seq (684 tracks)
- Histone modifications (1,860 tracks)
- TF ChIP-Seq (2,131 tracks)
- CAGE / gene expression
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Total:** ~5,300 epigenomic outputs from a single model
:::
:::

::: {.source-credit-linked}
Avsek, Z. et al. Nat Methods (2021). doi:10.1038/s41592-021-01252-x
:::

---

## The input: 200 kilobases of DNA

Enformer takes a **200 kb** DNA sequence as input:

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```
...AGTTC...TAGTTCC... (200,000 bp)
          |
     prediction target
     (center of window)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Why 200 kb?**

- Regulatory elements (enhancers) can be **hundreds of kb** away from the genes they control
- A model with a large **receptive field** can capture long-range dependencies
:::
:::

---

## Step 1: One-hot encoding

Just like in Unit 00, DNA is converted to a numeric matrix:

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```
A → [1, 0, 0, 0]
C → [0, 1, 0, 0]
G → [0, 0, 1, 0]
T → [0, 0, 0, 1]
```

Input shape: **4 × 196,608**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- 4 channels (one per nucleotide)
- ~197K positions (padded to 196,608)
- Same encoding you learned in Unit 00!
:::
:::

---

## Step 2: The CNN backbone — 17 convolutional layers

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
The sequence passes through a **deep 1D CNN**:

| Layer | Filters | Kernel |
|-------|---------|--------|
| 1–2 | 512 | 8 |
| 3–17 | 512 | varies (3–13) |
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Key design:**

- **Dilated convolutions** expand the receptive field exponentially
- Final receptive field: **131,072 bp** (~131 kb)
- Captures motifs and long-range dependencies
:::
:::

::: {.source-credit-linked}
Avsek et al. Nat Methods (2021)
:::

---

## Receptive field: why it matters

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
The **receptive field** determines how much of the input sequence each output position can "see":

- A shallow CNN might see only 1 kb
- Enformer sees **~131 kb**
- This is critical for capturing enhancer → promoter interactions
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```
Input (200 kb):    ACGT...[131 kb window]...ACGT
                              |
                    CNN layers
                              |
                    Output:   [prediction]
```
:::
:::

::: {.source-credit-linked}
Avsek et al. Nat Methods (2021)
:::

---

## Step 3: The dense (attention-like) layer

After the CNN, Enformer adds a **dense layer that models interactions between all output positions**:

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
This is the **most computationally expensive** part:

- 4,096 bins × 4,096 bins
- Captures **long-range relationships** between distant genomic positions
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Think of it as:

> "Which parts of the sequence, even far apart, jointly determine the output?"
:::
:::

::: {.source-credit-linked}
Avsek et al. Nat Methods (2021)
:::

---

## Step 4: Output heads

The model produces predictions for each epigenomic track:

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Output shape:** 4,096 bins × N tracks

- 4,096 = number of output positions (downsampled from 196,608)
- N = number of tracks (up to 5,313)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Each bin covers ~48 bp of the genome.

Predictions are compared to **observed** epigenomic signal (e.g., from ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics).
:::
:::

::: {.source-credit-linked}
Avsek et al. Nat Methods (2021)
:::

---

## Enformer in one picture

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
```
DNA Sequence (200 kb)
       |
       v
+-------------+
| One-hot     |  4 x 196,608
| encoding    |
+-----+-------+
      |
      v
+-------------+
| 17x 1D CNN  |  dilated convolutions
| backbone    |  receptive field ~131 kb
+-----+-------+
      |
      v
+-------------+
| Dense layer |  position interactions
+-----+-------+
      |
      v
+-------------+
| Output      |  4,096 bins x N tracks
| heads       |  DNase, histone, TF, CAGE
+-------------+
```
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
**Key numbers:**

- Input: 200 kb
- Receptive field: 131 kb
- Outputs: ~5,300 tracks
- Parameters: ~336 million
:::
:::

::: {.source-credit-linked}
Avsek et al. Nat Methods (2021)
:::

---

## How well does Enformer work?

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Genome-wide prediction:**

- Strong correlation between predicted and observed epigenomic signals
- Works across cell types and tissues
- Predicts gene expression (CAGE) well
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Variant effect prediction:**

- Can compare reference vs. alternative allele predictions
- Identifies functional non-coding variants
- But: **population-level** prediction is more challenging
:::
:::

::: {.source-credit-linked}
Avsek et al. Nat Methods (2021)
:::

---

## A key limitation: cross-individual prediction

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
Enformer was trained to perform well **across the genome** for a reference individual.

**But we often want to know:**

> "How does this variant change the epigenome in *this person* vs. *that person*?"
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
This requires:

- Predicting for **many different genomes** (not just one)
- Each prediction is computationally expensive
- The model doesn't explicitly model genetic variation
:::
:::

---

# Part 2: Beyond Enformer — Borzoi, AlphaGenome & More {background-color="#1e3a5f" style="color:white;"}

---

## Borzoi: a faster, larger model

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Borzoi** (Inoue et al., 2022):

- Uses **Transformer** architecture instead of CNN
- Trained on 5,500+ chromatin profiles
- Can predict **cell-type-specific** effects
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Key difference:**

- Transformer attention captures global context
- More interpretable (attention maps show which regions matter)
:::
:::

::: {.source-credit-linked}
Inoue, A. et al. Nat Genet (2022)
:::

---

## AlphaGenome: the next generation

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**AlphaGenome** (Avsek et al., 2025):

- Successor to Enformer
- Built on the **AlphaFold** architecture philosophy
- Unified model for regulatory variant effect prediction
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Improvements:**

- Better variant effect prediction
- More accurate across diverse populations
- Larger receptive field
:::
:::

::: {.source-credit-linked}
Avsek, Z. et al. bioRxiv (2025)
:::

---

## The landscape of DNA-sequence-to-function models

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
| Model | Year | Architecture | Output |
|-------|------|-------------|--------|
| **Enformer** | 2021 | CNN + dense | 5,300 epigenomic tracks |
| **Borzoi** | 2022 | Transformer | Chromatin profiles |
| **AlphaGenome** | 2025 | AlphaFold-style | Regulatory variants |
| **Nucleosome** | 2022 | CNN | Nucleosome positioning |
| **Basset** | 2016 | CNN | Chromatin accessibility |
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Common thread:**

All take raw DNA sequence as input and predict some functional output — no experiment needed.
:::
:::

---

## Why this matters for genomics

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Before these models:**

- Functional annotation required expensive experiments
- Each assay = one cell type, one condition
- Population studies required thousands of samples
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**With these models:**

- Predict any epigenomic signal from sequence alone
- In silico mutagenesis: test every possible variant
- Scale to population-level studies without new experiments
:::
:::

---

::: {.columns}

**Unit 01:** You trained a Transformer on DNA sequences
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

## Summary

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Most disease variants are in **non-coding** DNA
- They likely act by altering **regulatory elements** (TF binding, chromatin)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Enformer** predicts thousands of epigenomic signals from 200 kb of DNA sequence
- **Borzoi, AlphaGenome** and others extend this idea
- These models enable **in silico** functional genomics at scale
:::
:::
